Subject: Middle East crude exports recover but logistical and refining bottlenecks persist

Hi Callum,

I’m Sean Walker, working on EMRADAR, a system that tracks emerging market formations from evidence in the real economy.

Our 6 October scan identified a durable energy-logistics and refining bottleneck supporting high delivered fuel costs despite improving crude export volumes. The formation is CONFIRMED. What stood out was the divergence between recovered crude exports and constraints in tanker capacity, insurance, refining outages, and inventory replenishment. 

We are developing an evidence-backed contribution around distinguishing recovered crude exports from usable refining capacity and accessible product inventories — while keeping unresolved refinery restoration schedules, duration of tanker risk, fuel price pass-through, and inventory quality and location explicit. 

Would this be suitable as an article or research contribution for Hydrocarbon Engineering? 

If useful, I can send a concise finished draft with sources for review.

Regards,
Sean Walker
EMRADAR

source_facts.text: Aramco's CEO said nearly 3 billion barrels of gross supply had been lost, more than 1 billion barrels had been drawn from stocks and replenishment could take up to two years.
UKMTO recorded repeated tanker attacks and a 5 October incident in which a tanker was instructed to turn back or be targeted.
Reuters reports Middle East exports briefly exceeded pre-war levels while tanker attacks and logistical constraints continued.
Reuters reports VLCC rates above US$1.2 million per day versus roughly US$30,000 in January and freight rising from about 3% to 27% of delivered barrel cost.

source_uncertainty: Crude export recovery could alleviate some upstream tightness.
Industry executives have commercial incentives to emphasise scarcity and high prices.
War-risk data can change rapidly and some ship movements are obscured by disabled tracking.

Subject: Energy logistics bottleneck deepens despite crude export recovery

Hi John,

I’m Sean Walker, working on EMRADAR, a system that tracks emerging market formations from evidence in the real economy.

Our 6 October scan identified a durable energy-logistics and refining bottleneck as CONFIRMED. What stood out was that longer routes and ship-to-ship transfers continue impacting operational tanker availability distinctly from crude production. 

We are developing an evidence-backed contribution around this maritime logistics angle — while keeping unresolved issues such as the duration of tanker risk, refinery restoration schedules, fuel price pass-through, and accessible inventory quality explicit. 

Would this be suitable as an article or research contribution for Riviera Maritime Media / Tanker Shipping & Trade? 

If useful, I can send a concise finished draft with sources for review.

Regards,
Sean Walker
EMRADAR

Subject: Middle East crude export recovery reveals tanker and refining bottlenecks

Hi Julian,

I’m Sean Walker, working on EMRADAR, a system that tracks emerging market formations from evidence in the real economy.

Our 6 October scan identified a durable energy-logistics and refining bottleneck is supporting high delivered fuel costs even when crude export volumes improve. The formation is CONFIRMED. What stood out was safe tanker capacity and war-risk insurance distinguish recovered crude flows from delivered fuel availability. 

We are developing an evidence-backed contribution around how repeated tanker attacks, prolonged routes, damaged refineries, and depleted inventories elevate freight and fuel prices — while keeping unresolved issues such as tanker risk duration, refinery repair schedules, fuel pass-through, and accessible inventory location explicit. 

Would this be suitable as an article or research contribution for TradeWinds? 

If useful, I can send a concise finished draft with sources for review.

Regards,
Sean Walker
